newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire troops thwart anti-Mobutu march in capital.
newsitem.headline: Zaire troops thwart anti-Mobutu march in capital.

text.p: Opponents of President Mobutu Sese Seko paralysed Zaire's capital for a second day on Tuesday but troops blocked a potentially more disruptive student march.

On the diplomatic front, Laurent Kabila's rebels, who now control half of the huge Central African nation, including its mineral-rich economic heart, faced growing pressure to return to the negotiating table.
In Kinshasa, a government spokesman said former prime minister Kengo wa Dondo had fled the country and that judicial proceedings were being prepared against him and some key aides.

Paramilitary security forces blocked off access roads to Kinshasa's volatile campuses, where anti-Mobutu students skipped classes at the request of the main opposition, which also called for a drive-by protest to follow a stay-at-home action on Monday.
Although students were unable to gather in large numbers or protest through the streets of Kinshasa, opposition leaders claimed victory by the fact that most of the capital remained at a standstill.
"We have done what we wanted to do. People did not go to work. The people listened to us," said opposition spokesman Laurent Mabyo.
But a government spokesman dismissed, the claim, saying the authorities had demonstrated that emergency rule clamped on the country by Mobutu last week were working.
"There was no march because students were afraid they would be arrested," said Leon Kalima, a spokesman for emergency-rule Prime Minister General Likulia Bolongo.
"People stayed at home not because of compliance with the opposition order but because they were afraid of being attacked by militants," Kalima told Reuters.

Witnesses said students did not appear to make any special effort to march. Some residents said this reflected a feeling that there was no point risking a clash with troops while rebels were already closing in on Mobutu's last stronghold.
By late afternoon, the city of over five million people had cautiously regained much of its usual bustle although offices and shops remained largely closed.
South Africa's deputy foreign minister told a parliamentary committee in Cape Town that Zaire could be on the brink of formal negotiations about a transition to democracy.

"What has happened in an interesting way in the last few days is that both parties have signalled their commitment to meet directly at the principal level in order to negotiate the future dispensation in Zaire," Aziz Pahad said.
In Kinshasa, gendarmerie units directed traffic on the central November 24 Avenue, on which are located two flashpoint campuses, notably the Higher Institute of Commerce.
Witnesses said most troops had concentrated at the Gaba roundabout leading to the main University of Kinshasa campus.
Supporters of ousted prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi, Mobutu's arch political rival, have resorted to protests while Kabila's rebels pursue an armed campaign from eastern Zaire.
Tshisekedi supporters shut down the teeming capital with a widely observed stay-at-home order on Monday.

Pro-Tshisekedi protest organisers asked students to skip school and college on Tuesday and to turn out in vehicles. In the past, such protests have led to turmoil as students commandeered any vehicles on the street.
Mobutu, 66, declared a state of emergency last week and named an army prime minister, General Bolongo, shunting aside Tshisekedi after less than a week in the job.
